'''Adam Guy Riess''' (born December 16, 1969) is an American [[astrophysics|astrophysicist]] and [[Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|Bloomberg Distinguished Professor]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]] and the [[Space Telescope Science Institute]]. He is known for his research in using [[supernovae]] as cosmological probes. Riess shared both the 2006 [[Shaw Prize|Shaw Prize in Astronomy]] and the [[2011 Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Saul Perlmutter]] and [[Brian Schmidt]] for providing evidence that the [[Accelerating universe|expansion of the universe is accelerating]].

Riess has been at the center of a growing scientific debate about the so-called “Hubble tension” &mdash; a discrepancy between measurements of the universe’s expansion rate using nearby supernovae, and measurements inferred from the cosmic microwave background radiation using the [[Physical cosmology#Standard model of Big Bang cosmology|Standard Model of cosmology]]. Riess’s data has prompted questions and further testing to determine if the Standard Model still adequately describes the universe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Andersen |first=Ross |date=2025-05-30 |title=The Nobel Prize Winner Who Thinks We Have the Universe All Wrong |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2025/05/adam-riess-hubble-tension/682980/ |access-date=2025-06-01 |website=The Atlantic |language=en}}</ref>

==Family==
Riess was born to a [[Jewish]] family in [[Washington, D.C.]], and grew up in [[Warren Township, New Jersey]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.haaretz.com/us-news/jewish-insider-s-daily-kickoff-december-15-2017-1.5628773|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817211811/https://www.haaretz.com/us-news/jewish-insider-s-daily-kickoff-december-15-2017-1.5628773|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 17, 2019|title = Jewish Insider's Daily Kickoff: December 15, 2017|newspaper = Haaretz}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=WEDDINGS; Nancy Schondorf And Adam Riess|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/01/11/style/weddings-nancy-schondorf-and-adam-riess.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=January 11, 1998}}</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/18/style/dr-gail-riess-is-married.html Wedding: Drs. Gail Michele Riess and Leonard Bruce Saltz]. Nytimes.com (June 18, 1989). Retrieved on April 2, 2012.</ref> He has two sisters: [[Gail Saltz]], a psychiatrist, and Holly Hagerman, an artist.

His father, Michael Riess (1931–2007), served in the [[U.S. Navy]] and later owned a frozen-foods distribution company; his mother, Doris Riess, worked as a clinical psychologist.<ref>[http://www.jhu.edu/jhumag/0208web/riess.html Chasing the Great Beyond] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120628101901/http://www.jhu.edu/jhumag/0208web/riess.html |date=June 28, 2012 }}. Jhu.edu (January 12, 1998). Retrieved on April 2, 2012.</ref> His paternal grandfather was the journalist and war correspondent [[Curt Martin Riess]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Saxon|first=Wolfgang|title=Curt Riess, Author And Journalist, 90; Expert on Nazi Era|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/05/21/obituaries/curt-riess-author-and-journalist-90-expert-on-nazi-era.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=May 21, 1993}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Obituary: Michael Riess |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 11, 2007 |access-date=April 2, 2012 |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage-9E07E3DD163AF932A25753C1A9619C8B63.html}}</ref>

Riess married Nancy Joy Schondorf in 1998. They have two children, Noah and Gabrielle.

==Education==
He attended [[Watchung Hills Regional High School]], graduating in the class of 1988.<ref>Spivey, Mark. [http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20160523200519/http://m.dailyrecord.com/topnews/article?a=2011310040033&f=847 "Watchung Hills graduate shares Nobel Prize in physics"], ''[[Daily Record (Morristown)]]'', October 4, 2011. Accessed October 5, 2011. "Riess, who grew up in Warren, gave a shout-out to retired teacher Jeff Charney, saying his interest in science first was piqued at Watchung Hills."</ref> He also attended the prestigious New Jersey Governor's School in the Sciences in 1987. Riess then graduated Phi Beta Kappa from [[The Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1992 where he was a member of the [[Phi Delta Theta]] fraternity. He received his [[PhD#United States|PhD]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1996; it resulted in measurements of over twenty new [[Type Ia supernovae]] and a method to utilize Type Ia supernovae as accurate distance indicators by correcting for intervening dust and intrinsic inhomogeneities. Riess's PhD thesis was supervised by [[Robert Kirshner]] and [[William H. Press]] and won the [[Robert J. Trumpler Award]] in 1999 for PhD theses of unusual importance to astronomy.<ref>{{cite book |last=Panek |first=Richard |title=The 4% Universe: Dark Matter, Dark Energy, and the Race to Discover the Rest of Reality |year=2011 |publisher=[[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt]] |location=Boston |isbn=978-0-618-98244-8}}, pg. 174</ref>

==Research==
Riess was a [[Miller Fellow]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], from 1996 through 1999, during which period his first seminal paper on the discovery of an accelerating universe was published.<ref name=jhu20160708>Messersmith, Julie. [http://hub.jhu.edu/2016/07/08/adam-riess-bloomberg-distinguished-professor "Nobel laureate Adam Riess named 22nd Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins"], ''JHU Hub'', Baltimore, 8 July 2016. Retrieved on 13 July 2016.</ref>  In 1999, he moved to the [[Space Telescope Science Institute]] and took up a position at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 2006. He also sits on the selection committee for the Astronomy award given under the auspices of the [[Shaw Prize]]. In July 2016, Riess was named a [[Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships|Bloomberg Distinguished Professor]] at Johns Hopkins University for his accomplishments as an interdisciplinary researcher and excellence in teaching the next generation of scholars.<ref name=jhu20160708 /> The Bloomberg Distinguished Professorships were established in 2013 by a gift from [[Michael Bloomberg]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Michael R. Bloomberg Commits $350 Million to Johns Hopkins for Transformational Academic Initiative 2013|url= http://releases.jhu.edu/2013/01/26/michael-r-bloomberg-commits-350-million-to-johns-hopkins/}}</ref>

Riess jointly led the study with [[Brian Schmidt]] in 1998 for the [[High-z Supernova Search Team]] which first reported evidence that the universe's expansion rate is accelerating through monitoring of Type Ia supernovae. The team's observations were contrary to the existing theory that the expansion of the universe was slowing down; instead, by monitoring the color shifts in the light from supernovae from Earth, they discovered that these billion-year old novae were still accelerating.<ref name="bbc nobel"/> This result was also found nearly simultaneously by the [[Supernova Cosmology Project]], led by [[Saul Perlmutter]].<ref name="bbc nobel">{{cite web | url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-15165371 | title = Nobel physics prize honours accelerating Universe find | first =Jason | last = Palmer | date = October 4, 2011 | access-date = October 5, 2011 | publisher = [[BBC]] }}</ref> The corroborating evidence between the two competing studies led to the acceptance of the [[accelerating universe]] theory, and initiated new research to understand the nature of the universe, such as the existence of [[dark energy]].<ref name="bbc nobel"/> The discovery of the accelerating universe was named 'Breakthrough of the Year' by ''Science'' magazine in 1998,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bloom|first=Floyd E. |title=Breakthroughs 1998 |journal=Science |date=18 Dec 1998 |volume=282 |issue=5397 |page=2193 |doi=10.1126/science.282.5397.2193 |bibcode=1998Sci...282.2193B |s2cid=220092189 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.282.5397.2193 |access-date=27 November 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Riess was jointly awarded the [[2011 Nobel Prize in Physics]] along with Schmidt and Perlmutter for their groundbreaking work.<ref name="bbc nobel"/>

From 2002 to 2007 Riess led the Higher-Z SN Team which used the Hubble Space Telescope to find dozens of type Ia supernovae at z>1, first demonstrating that the expansion of the Universe was decelerating before it began accelerating and ruling out astrophysical contamination of SN Ia.<ref>[https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004ApJ...607..665R/abstract Type Ia Supernova Discoveries at z > 1 from the Hubble Space Telescope]</ref>

Riess is also known for his efforts to measure the local value of the Hubble constant while leading the SH0ES Team since 2005 with measurements that approach 1% precision and which indicate a discrepancy with the model-based prediction from the CMB, a problem widely known in cosmology as the [[Hubble's law|Hubble tension]].<ref>
[https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...826...56R/abstract A 2.4% Determination of the Local Value of the Hubble Constant]</ref><ref>[https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...934L...7R/abstract A Comprehensive Measurement of the Local Value of the Hubble Constant with 1 km s-1 Mpc-1 Uncertainty from the Hubble Space Telescope and the SH0ES Team]</ref>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Shaw2006astro.jpg|thumb|[[Saul Perlmutter]], Riess, and [[Brian P. Schmidt]] being awarded the 2006 [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy. The trio would later be awarded the [[2011 Nobel Prize in Physics]].]]

Riess received the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]]'s [[Robert J. Trumpler Award]] in 1999 and [[Harvard University]]'s Bok Prize in 2001. He won  the American Astronomical Society's [[Helen B. Warner Prize]] in 2003 and the Raymond and Beverly [[Sackler Prize]] in Physics in 2004 for the discovery of cosmic acceleration.<ref name="Sackler International Prize in Physics 2004">{{cite web | title=Past Laureates of the Raymond and Beverly Sackler International Prize in Physics | website=Tel Aviv University | date=2012-09-05 | url=https://english.tau.ac.il/sackler_prize_in_physics_past_laureates | access-date=2023-05-28 | archive-date=October 16, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016014757/https://english.tau.ac.il/sackler_prize_in_physics_past_laureates | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2006, he shared the $1&nbsp;million [[Shaw Prize]] in [[Astronomy]] with [[Saul Perlmutter]] and [[Brian P. Schmidt]] for contributions to the discovery of the [[accelerating universe|acceleration of the universe]].<ref name="BBC">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-15165371|title=Nobel physics prize honours accelerating Universe find|work=[[BBC News]]|date=October 4, 2011}}</ref>

Schmidt and all the members of the High-Z Team (as defined by the co-authors of Riess et al. 1998) shared the 2007 [[Gruber Prize in Cosmology|Gruber Cosmology Prize]], a $500,000 award, with the Supernova Cosmology Project (the set defined by the co-authors of Perlmutter et al. 1999) for their discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe. Riess was the winner of MacArthur "Genius" Grant in 2008. He was also elected in 2009 to the National Academy of Sciences.<ref>[https://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=04282009 Newsroom]. National-Academies.org (April 28, 2009). Retrieved on April 2, 2012.</ref>

Along with Perlmutter and Schmidt, he was awarded the 2011 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] for his contributions to the discovery of the acceleration of the expansion of the universe.<ref name="BBC" />

Riess, along with [[Brian P. Schmidt]], and the [[High-Z Supernova Search Team]] shared in the 2015 [[Fundamental Physics Prize|Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]].<ref name=" Breakthrough Prize Adam Riess">{{cite web | title=Breakthrough Prize – Fundamental Physics Breakthrough Prize Laureates – Adam Riess and the High-z Supernova Search Team | website= Breakthrough Prize | url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L73 | ref={{sfnref | Breakthrough Prize }} | access-date=2023-05-28}}</ref>

In 2012, Riess received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref>

In 2020, Riess was made fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2020/03/04/american-astronomical-society-fellows/|title=Four Johns Hopkins faculty members named American Astronomical Society fellows|date=2020-03-04|website=The Hub|publisher=Johns Hopkins University|language=en|access-date=2020-03-06}}</ref>

== Media appearances ==
Riess participated on the [[NPR]] radio quiz program ''[[Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me!]]'' in 2011.<ref>[https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=199102680 Wait Wait...Don't Tell Me!] from [[National Public Radio|NPR]]</ref>

== Publications ==
Riess has more than 137,000 citations in Google Scholar and an h-index of 130. His most cited work, "Observational evidence from supernovae for an accelerating universe and a cosmological constant," has been cited over 28,000 times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Adam Riess|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=geafuP0AAAAJ&hl=en|access-date=2021-05-19|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref> Riess has been among the top 1% most cited in the world for subject field and year of publication in the [[Thomson Reuters]] Highly Cited Researchers reports for multiple years, including 2014-2016 and 2020-2023.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-11-18|title=13 Johns Hopkins scientists among most cited researchers in the world|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2016/11/18/highly-cited-researchers/|access-date=2021-05-19|website=The Hub|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Adam G. Riess|url=https://clarivate.com/webofsciencegroup/citation-laureates/resources/adam-g-riess/|access-date=2021-05-19|website=Web of Science Group|date=September 21, 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

* [https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=geafuP0AAAAJ&hl=en Google Scholar citations]

* 2009 with KN Abazajian, JK Adelman-McCarthy, MA Agüeros, SS Allam, CA Prieto, et al., ''The seventh data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series''. Vol. 182, nº 2; 543.
* 2004 with LG Strolger, J Tonry, S Casertano, HC Ferguson, B Mobasher, et al., ''Type Ia supernova discoveries at z> 1 from the Hubble Space Telescope: Evidence for past deceleration and constraints on dark energy evolution'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal''. Vol. 607, nº 2; 665.
* 2009 with KN Abazajian, JK Adelman-McCarthy, MA Agüeros, SS Allam, CA Prieto, et al., ''The seventh data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series''. Vol. 182, nº 2; 543.
* 2003 with JL Tonry, BP Schmidt, B Barris, P Candia, P Challis, A Clocchiatti, AL Coil, et al., ''Cosmological results from high-z supernovae'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal''. Vol. 594, nº 1; 1.
* 2007 with LG Strolger, S Casertano, HC Ferguson, B Mobasher, B Gold, et al., ''New Hubble space telescope discoveries of type Ia supernovae at z≥ 1: narrowing constraints on the early behavior of dark energy'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal''. Vol. 659, nº 1; 98.
* 1998 with BP Schmidt, NB Suntzeff, MM Phillips, RA Schommer, A Clocchiatti, et al., ''The high-Z supernova search: measuring cosmic deceleration and global curvature of the universe using type Ia supernovae'', in: ''The Astrophysical Journal''. Vol. 507, nº 1; 46.
